name: op_accessibility_action_focus
description: ACCESSIBILITY ACTIONS, the first scenario in the corpus that touches them at all. `LayoutWindow::process_accessibility_action` — focus moves, scroll offsets, expand/collapse, text replacement, and the action -> EventFilter mapping that turns a screen reader's activation into a callback — was reachable from exactly one place: a live AT-SPI / UIA / NSAccessibility connection. No test has one. That is how 'a screen reader activates a button and no callback runs' shipped, and it is why iOS, Android and headless could go all the way to release with NO `process_accessibility_actions` implementation at all and nothing anywhere going red. The `accessibility_action` op is the door: it addresses a node the way an assistive technology does (by identity + action name, not by pointer coordinate) and pushes `CallbackChange::PerformAccessibilityAction`, i.e. the SAME change the platform pumps apply. BEAT 1 — `focus` on #f2. `AccessibilityAction::Focus` calls `focus_manager.set_focused_node` directly, so `get_focus_state` must now name f2; a no-op action leaves focus empty and `assert_response` goes red on the missing id. BEAT 2 — `focus` on #f3, proving the action re-targets rather than latching on the first node it ever saw. BEAT 3 — `blur`, which must clear the focus manager: `has_focus` false. That beat is the one that cannot be faked by an implementation that only ever sets focus. NOT COVERED HERE, deliberately and not silently: `default` (activation), which maps to a synthetic MouseUp on the target so the node's click callback runs. A JSON scenario cannot attach a Rust callback to a node — no op in the set binds one — so no scenario in this corpus can observe ANY user callback firing, a11y or otherwise. Focus/blur are the part of the action surface that JSON can prove, and they are proven here.
